people.name: Herwart Holland-Moritz
people.roles: hacker · journalist · Chaos Computer Club co-founder

keyWork.title: The Btx hack (with Steffen Wernéry), exposing the Bundespost's Bildschirmtext service

people.contribution: Holland was one of five Hamburg media activists who, in a notice in the Berlin newspaper taz on 1 September 1981, invited 'Komputerfrieks' to the 12 September 1981 meeting that the Chaos Computer Club counts as its informal founding. In November 1984 he and Steffen Wernéry used a Hamburger Sparkasse login to run up DM 134,634.88 on a CCC page in the Bundespost's Btx system, then went public to show the service was insecure. He lectured for years on people caught between media technology and surveillance, and died on 29 July 2001.
people.quote: Our common interest is not the protection of data, but the protection of people from data misuse.

quoteSource.title: 40 years ago: the Btx hack celebrates a happy birthday
quoteSource.quote: Our common interest is not the protection of data, but the protection of people from data misuse.
quoteSource.note: Holland's words to data-protection officials at the DAFTA conference, early November 1984, as quoted (in heise's English translation of Detlef Borchers's German article) from the CCC's own 1984 Btx dossier, a scanned PDF hosted by the Wau Holland Stiftung: https://www.wauland.de/media/btx-hack/1984-10-xx_CCC-Btx.pdf (no text layer; German original not checked).

people.influence: Friends and journalists credit Holland with fixing the pattern of CCC actions: expose a flaw, then go to the press to warn about weak security and insufficient data protection, which cast hackers in German public life as defenders of informational self-determination rather than computer criminals.
people.thread: The 1981 taz notice that called the first meeting already listed 'Datenrecht (Wem gehören meine Daten?)' — data law: who owns my data? — among the topics to discuss.

sources.quote: Unter dem Pseudonym Tom Twiddlebit verbarg sich Klaus Schleisiek, Wau stand für Herwart Holland-Moritz, genannt Wau Holland, mit Wolf war Wolf Gevert gemeint.

The thesis (pp. 57-60) reprints the taz notice 'TUWAT,TXT Version' (taz, 1 September 1981, p. 2), whose topic list includes 'Kommunikationsrecht – Datenrecht (Wem gehören meine Daten?)'.

sources.title: Hacker remembered as computer age hero / Wau Holland fought to free information
sources.quote: Whenever the CCC hacked into regions he wasn't supposed to see, he sought protection by seeking public attention, and used them to warn of weak security and insufficient data protection.
sources.note: Words of Holland's friend Boris Groendahl, quoted from his obituary in the Industry Standard.

sources.title: BTX Hack 30th Year Anniversary
sources.quote: This positive image of the hacker as "good people" who stand for data protection and informational self-determination has stayed the same to this day.
sources.note: The foundation's German 'about' page (https://www.wauland.de/de/about/) gives his death date: 'bis zu seinem Tod am 29. Juli 2001'.

events.title: 'Komputerfrieks' meet at the taz and the Chaos Computer Club is born
events.place: Editorial offices of die tageszeitung (taz), Wattstraße, Berlin-Wedding, West Berlin
events.summary: A notice headed 'TUWAT,TXT Version' in the taz of 1 September 1981, signed by five Hamburg media activists including Wau Holland and Klaus Schleisiek, invited computer enthusiasts to meet at the paper's Wattstraße building on 12 September 1981. About 20 people came, meeting around a large table that had once stood in the Kommune 1. The Chaos Computer Club counts this meeting as its informal founding; its topic list included data law under the question 'who owns my data?'.
events.significance: Europe's most influential hacker club began by asking, before most people owned a computer, who owns personal data.

events.title: The Btx hack: the Chaos Computer Club 'robs' a Hamburg savings bank to prove a point
events.summary: Overnight on 16–17 November 1984, Steffen Wernéry and Wau Holland of the Chaos Computer Club logged into the Deutsche Bundespost's new Bildschirmtext (Btx) service with the Hamburger Sparkasse's ID and password and had a program call a CCC page priced at DM 9.97 13,504 times, a virtual DM 134,634.88. The club had written to data-protection officials and the Bundespost about flaws in October 1984; after the hack its press release called for a ban on financial transactions on Btx. The 'bank robbery' made the CCC famous overnight.
events.significance: Established the hacker as a public-interest auditor of data protection: expose the flaw, tell the press, give the money back.

sources.title: 40 years ago: the Btx hack celebrates a happy birthday
sources.quote: On the night in question, the program clicked 13,504 times, totaling 13,504 × 9.97 DM = 134,634.88 DM.
sources.note: Also FOUND on the page: 'At night from November 16 to 17, 1984, two members of the "Btx editorial team" of the Chaos Computer Club (CCC) dialed into the new Btx system via the local network of the Deutsche Bundespost using the ID and password of the Hamburger Sparkasse.' The article links the CCC's press release of 19 November 1984 (https://wauland.de/media/btx-hack/1984-11-19_PM-CCC.pdf, scanned). Also FOUND: 'The CCC therefore drew attention to the central problem in the statement and called for a "ban on financial transactions" on Btx.' and 'With this "bank robbery", the CCC suddenly became famous.'

sources.title: BTX Hack 30th Year Anniversary
sources.quote: In the night from 16 to 17 November 1984 the hacker world changed forever in Germany.
sources.note: The foundation rounds the sum to 'DM 135.000'; heise gives the exact DM 134,634.88.

events.locationNote: Hamburg, where Holland and Wernéry ran the hack and the club was based; exact building not established.

events.title: The Chaos Computer Club takes apart the German police 'state trojan'
events.summary: On 8 October 2011 the CCC published binaries and an analysis of 'lawful interception' malware used by German police, sent to it anonymously. It reported that software meant only to tap internet telephony could also take screenshots, load and run further programs and be taken over by third parties, because its commands were unencrypted and unauthenticated. The club argued this breached limits set by the Federal Constitutional Court in its 27 February 2008 ruling; Bavarian officials later confirmed using the software in five cases.
events.significance: Hackers, not a regulator, audited the state's own surveillance code and showed that a person's computer had become part of the 'core area of private life'.

sources.title: Chaos Computer Club analyzes government malware
sources.quote: The largest European hacker club, "Chaos Computer Club" (CCC), has reverse engineered and analyzed a "lawful interception" malware program used by German police forces.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'The CCC demands: The clandestine infiltration of IT systems by government agencies must stop.' The release refers to the Bundesverfassungsgericht decision of 27 February 2008 (1 BvR 370/07).

sources.title: Chaos Computer Club: German gov't software can spy on citizens
sources.quote: Security firm F-Secure will detect and disable the alleged government monitoring software if found on clients' computers, it announced on Saturday.
sources.note: Published 8 October 2011 (datePublished in page metadata), the day of the CCC release.

sources.title: How the German "Federal Trojan" was actually used
sources.quote: According to Bavarian newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (via Google Translate), Bavarian law enforcement agents used it in five different cases, none of which falls under the above mentioned category.
sources.note: Secondary report relaying the Süddeutsche Zeitung.

events.locationNote: The CCC is a registered association seated in Hamburg; the analysis was published on ccc.de.
